items.premise: The new Vmar::protect documentation states a surprising partial-failure behavior but does not cite or explain the source/rationale for that behavior.
evidence: kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/protect.rs:13-16 documents ENOMEM for unmapped pages and partial protection before the hole, but the only link-style reference is [`ENOMEM`]: Errno::ENOMEM; there is no source/rationale citation for the partial side effect.

kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/protect.rs:30-37 detects a gap before the next mapping and returns Errno::ENOMEM; because the loop protects earlier mappings at lines 46-63 before later gaps are detected, the partial side effect is implemented.

Linux mm/mprotect.c do_mprotect_pkey processes each VMA with mprotect_fixup before advancing; it reports -ENOMEM on a gap either when vma->vm_start != tmp or after the loop if tmp < end (kernel.googlesource.com torvalds/linux mm/mprotect.c lines 821-877).
Linux man-pages mprotect(2) documents ENOMEM when addresses in the requested range are invalid or one or more pages are not mapped (man7.org mprotect(2), ERRORS lines 117-120).
items.reason: The code and documentation show the partial ENOMEM behavior is implemented and documented without a source/rationale citation, and Linux sources/man-pages provide relevant external semantics.

items.premise: A next pre-collected mapping can be removed by `insert_try_merge(taken)` and then later still reach `inner.remove(&vm_mapping_range.start).unwrap()`, causing a kernel panic from user input.
evidence: kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/protect.rs:40-46 checks `if perms == vm_mapping_perms & VmPerms::ALL_PERMS { continue; }` before calling `inner.remove(...).unwrap()`.
kernel/src/vm/vmar/vm_mapping.rs:681-704 shows a protected mapping is reinserted with `perms` equal to the requested new permissions passed to `VmMapping::protect`.
kernel/src/vm/vmar/vm_mapping.rs:859-866 shows mappings can merge only if they are adjacent and have exactly equal `left.perms == right.perms` plus matching attributes.

In the described RW | R | RW then mprotect-all-to-RW case, the later right-hand RW mapping has old access permissions equal to the requested permissions, so its stale pre-collected entry would hit the line-40 `continue` before the line-46 `unwrap`, even if it had been merged/removed earlier.
items.reason: A mapping that can be merged into the just-protected mapping must already have the requested access permissions, and such stale entries are skipped before the unwrap; the provided panic path is not reachable as stated.

items.premise: The implementation now exposes msync ENOMEM behavior for ranges containing unmapped pages, but the Linux Compatibility docs and msync.scml were not updated to reflect it.
evidence: kernel/src/syscall/msync.rs:35-43 queries the VMAR and returns Errno::ENOMEM when `query_guard.is_fully_mapped()` is false.
kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/query.rs:32-50 defines `is_fully_mapped()` to return false exactly when the queried range contains unmapped pages, including holes and trailing unmapped regions.

book/src/kernel/linux-compatibility/syscall-flag-coverage/memory-management/README.md:40-52 contains the msync section but only lists supported SCML, the ignored MS_INVALIDATE flag, and the man-page link; it does not mention ENOMEM for unmapped pages.

book/src/kernel/linux-compatibility/syscall-flag-coverage/memory-management/msync.scml:1-10 only documents asynchronous/synchronous msync flag forms and does not document the unmapped-page ENOMEM behavior.
Linux man-pages msync(2) documents ENOMEM when the indicated memory, or part of it, was not mapped (man7.org msync(2), ERRORS lines 61-62).
items.reason: The syscall implementation includes the new full-mapping check and ENOMEM return, while the corresponding README and SCML entries contain no coverage of that behavior.

items.premise: The user-visible mprotect behavior for ranges with unmapped holes changed, but the Linux Compatibility README and mprotect.scml were not updated to describe ENOMEM and the partial effect.
evidence: kernel/src/syscall/mprotect.rs:46-49 invokes `vmar.protect(vm_perms, addr_range)` for the user-visible mprotect syscall.
kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/protect.rs:13-14 documents that unmapped pages cause ENOMEM and that pages before the unmapped hole are still protected.

kernel/src/vm/vmar/vmar_impls/protect.rs:30-37 and 46-63 implement the partial behavior: mappings encountered before a later gap are protected and reinserted, then a subsequent gap returns Errno::ENOMEM.

book/src/kernel/linux-compatibility/syscall-flag-coverage/memory-management/README.md:65-80 contains the mprotect section but only lists supported SCML, ignored protection flags, and the man-page link; it does not mention unmapped-range ENOMEM or partial permission changes.

book/src/kernel/linux-compatibility/syscall-flag-coverage/memory-management/mprotect.scml:1-11 only documents the prot argument values for mprotect and does not document the range-with-holes ENOMEM or partial side effect.
Linux man-pages mprotect(2) documents ENOMEM when addresses in the requested range are invalid or one or more pages are not mapped (man7.org mprotect(2), ERRORS lines 117-120).
items.reason: The syscall path exposes the new Vmar::protect behavior, and the compatibility documentation lacks any corresponding entry for unmapped holes or partial changes.
